desc:
The grid matrix holds non-negative integers. Among all rectangular blocks (consecutive rows and consecutive columns) whose cell sum is at least target, find the one with the smallest number of cells and return that number. If no block reaches target (not even the whole grid), return 0.

matrix = [[1, 2, 3],
          [4, 5, 6],
          [7, 8, 9]], target = 25
best block: the bottom-right 2 x 2 (5 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 28), area 4
result = 4
hints: Trying every block is O(R<sup>2</sup>C<sup>2</sup>) blocks. Fix the top and bottom rows to reduce the problem to one dimension.

For a fixed pair of rows, add the rows into one array of column sums. A block is now a contiguous segment of that array, and the width should be as small as possible while the segment sum is at least target.

All numbers are non-negative, so extending a segment never decreases its sum. That allows a two-pointer window over the column sums. Update the column sums incrementally while the bottom row moves down.
editorial: Fix the top row t and move the bottom row b downwards, maintaining col[c] = the sum of column c over rows t..b. Every block with these row bounds is a contiguous range of columns, with the sum of col over that range.

Because the values are non-negative, the shortest range ending at column right with sum at least target can be found with a sliding window: add col[right], and while the window sum is at least target, record the area (b - t + 1) * (right - left + 1) and drop the left column. Each column enters and leaves the window once.
This gives O(R<sup>2</sup> * C) time and O(C) space. With negative numbers the window would not be monotonic and a different technique (prefix sums with ordered lookups) would be required.
